intro: Hi! You can already talk about yesterday with went, saw and ate. Now you learn a new form for your experiences and for fresh news: I've been to Bali. I've just finished. Have you eaten yet? Warm-up: have you ever been to Bali? Try 'Yes, I have.' or 'No, I haven't.'
teachingNotes: Meaning: the present perfect (have/has + third form) is for something that happened before now when no finished time is said, and it matters now. This lesson uses it for two things only: experiences in your life (ever/never) and recent news (just/already/yet). Map it to Indonesian: pernah → ever (in questions), belum pernah → never, sudah → already, belum → not … yet, baru saja → just. 'Sudah makan (belum)?' → 'Have you eaten yet?'. Trap: 'Saya pernah ke Bali' is 'I have been to Bali' with NO ever: ever is for questions (*'I have ever been to Bali' is wrong).

Form: have with I/you/we/they, has with he/she/it (like 'Rina has a car' in the simple present), + the third form (past participle, 'bentuk ketiga'). Regular verbs: the third form looks the same as the past (work → worked → worked). The irregular ones that change, for this lesson: see → saw → seen, be → was/were → been, eat → ate → eaten, go → went → gone, do → did → done, write → wrote → written, take → took → taken. Same as the past: had, bought, made, said. Common errors: *'I have saw that film' (past instead of third form), *'She have finished', *'I has'. Short forms: I've, you've, we've, they've; he's/she's/it's = has when a third form follows (She's eaten) but = is before -ing (She's eating). 'I've had lunch' looks odd: the first have is the helper, had is the third form of have. Don't teach American 'gotten'.

Experiences: Have you ever + third form? Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. / No, never. never already means 'not', so *'I haven't never' is wrong. The node's common error *'Have you ever went to Japan?' → 'Have you ever been to Japan?': after have/has always the third form, and 'been to' = went there and came back (pernah ke). gone only as a note: 'Budi has gone to Bali' = he is in Bali now; 'Budi has been to Bali' = he went and came back.

just / already go between have/has and the third form (I've just arrived, She has already paid; already can also go at the end). yet goes at the end, in negatives and questions only (I haven't finished yet. Have you finished yet?). Short answers: Yes, I have. / No, not yet. The node's common error *'I already finish my homework' (no have, no -ed) → 'I've already finished my homework'. American English often uses the past simple here (I just ate. Did you eat yet?): accept it as American if the learner uses it, but teach and test the have/has form.

Contrast with the past simple, stated simply: a finished time (yesterday, last night, last week, last year, two days ago, a question with When?) needs the past simple: *'I have seen it yesterday' → 'I saw it yesterday'. Indonesian 'sudah' often appears with kemarin ('Kemarin saya sudah ke dokter'): that is still 'I went to the doctor yesterday'. A typical conversation starts with the present perfect and gives the details in the past simple: 'Have you ever been to Lombok? — Yes, I have. I went there last year.' Test this only with clear finished-time words.

Limits: don't teach for/since, How long…?, the present perfect continuous, still, recently, or unfinished time (this week, today, so far). Keep been vs gone as a note, not a test topic. No will, going to or comparatives (not in this lesson's chain). If the learner meets another irregular verb, just give its third form as a word to remember.

keyPoints.title: have/has + the third form
keyPoints.explanation: The present perfect is have/has + the third form of the verb (past participle). Use have with I, you, we, they and has with he, she, it. For regular verbs the third form looks like the past (worked, visited, finished). Some irregular verbs have a new third form: seen, been, eaten, gone, done, written, taken. Never use the past form here: I have seen, not 'I have saw'.

examples.en: We haven't seen the new office.

id.title: have/has + bentuk ketiga
id.explanation: Present perfect adalah have/has + bentuk ketiga kata kerja (past participle). Pakai have untuk I, you, we, they dan has untuk he, she, it. Untuk kata kerja beraturan, bentuk ketiganya sama dengan bentuk lampau (worked, visited, finished). Beberapa kata kerja tidak beraturan punya bentuk ketiga yang baru: seen, been, eaten, gone, done, written, taken. Jangan pakai bentuk lampau di sini: I have seen, bukan 'I have saw'.

keyPoints.title: Experiences: ever and never
keyPoints.explanation: To ask about someone's life, use Have you ever + third form? (ever = pernah). Answer: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Use never for 'belum pernah': I have never eaten durian. For places, say been to: Have you ever been to Bali? (been is the third form of be; went is the past). In a positive sentence there is no ever: Saya pernah ke Bali = I have been to Bali. When you say when it happened, use the past simple: I went there last year.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Lombok? — Yes, I have.
Dimas has been to Malaysia. He went there last year.
examples.id: Dimas pernah ke Malaysia. Dia ke sana tahun lalu.

id.title: Pengalaman: ever dan never
id.explanation: Untuk bertanya tentang pengalaman hidup seseorang, pakai Have you ever + bentuk ketiga? (ever = pernah). Jawabannya: Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Pakai never untuk 'belum pernah': I have never eaten durian. Untuk tempat, pakai been to: Have you ever been to Bali? (been adalah bentuk ketiga dari be; went itu bentuk lampau). Di kalimat positif tidak ada ever: Saya pernah ke Bali = I have been to Bali. Kalau kamu menyebut kapan terjadinya, pakai past simple: I went there last year.

keyPoints.title: just, already and yet
keyPoints.explanation: just = baru saja, already = sudah, yet = belum (in negatives) or sudah…belum? (in questions). just and already go between have/has and the third form: I've just arrived. She has already paid. yet goes at the end, only in negatives and questions: I haven't finished yet. Have you eaten yet? — No, not yet. Not 'I already finish': English needs have + third form.

examples.en: Have you eaten yet? — No, not yet.

id.title: just, already dan yet
id.explanation: just = baru saja, already = sudah, yet = belum (di kalimat negatif) atau sudah…belum? (di pertanyaan). just dan already diletakkan di antara have/has dan bentuk ketiga: I've just arrived. She has already paid. yet diletakkan di akhir, hanya di kalimat negatif dan pertanyaan: I haven't finished yet. Have you eaten yet? — No, not yet. Bukan 'I already finish': bahasa Inggris perlu have + bentuk ketiga.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with the present perfect of 'clean': We ___ the kitchen. It looks great now.
guidedPractice.hint: We → have. clean is regular: the third form is the same as the past.

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete with the present perfect of 'go': Pak Hasan isn't at his desk. He ___ to the bank.
Give a short answer (yes): Have you ever eaten rendang?
guidedPractice.hint: The question starts with Have you…, so answer with I + have.

guidedPractice.prompt: Make it negative and add 'yet': I have finished the report.
expected: i haven't finished the report yet
i have not finished the report yet
guidedPractice.hint: haven't + third form, and yet goes at the end.

independentPractice.hint: pernah ke = have been to. No ever in a positive sentence.

independentPractice.prompt: Translate with 'already': Dia (perempuan) sudah membeli tiketnya.
expected: she has already bought the ticket
she has already bought the tickets
she has bought the ticket already
she has bought the tickets already
independentPractice.hint: she → has. buy → bought → bought. already goes after has.

independentPractice.prompt: Make a question: Dimas has done his homework.
independentPractice.hint: Put Has before Dimas. The third form stays: done.

assessment.prompt: Complete with the present perfect of 'take': Rina ___ a lot of photos of the new office.
acceptableAnswers: has taken
's taken
assessment.rubric: Correct: has taken. 'has took' = 40 (past form instead of the third form, the node's main error). 'have taken' = 60 (Rina = she → has). 'has taked' = 30. 'took' = 30 (past simple, not the present perfect).

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: I have seen Dimas at the mall yesterday.
acceptableAnswers: i saw dimas at the mall yesterday
yesterday i saw dimas at the mall
assessment.rubric: Correct: I saw Dimas at the mall yesterday (yesterday is a finished time → past simple). Removing 'yesterday' and keeping 'I have seen Dimas at the mall' = 50 (grammatical, but the time was part of the message). 'I have saw' = 10. 'I see' = 20. Sentence unchanged = 0.

assessment.prompt: Write a question with 'ever' (Kamu pernah melihat komodo?): you / see / a Komodo dragon
acceptableAnswers: have you ever seen a komodo dragon
have you ever seen a komodo
have you ever seen komodo dragons
have you ever seen komodos
assessment.rubric: Correct: Have you ever seen a Komodo dragon? 'Have you ever saw' = 50 (past form instead of the third form). 'Did you ever see a Komodo dragon' = 50 (American past simple; this lesson asks for have + third form). 'You have ever seen…?' = 40 (statement order). 'Have you ever see' = 40.

assessment.prompt: Translate with 'never': Saya belum pernah ke Singapura.
acceptableAnswers: i have never been to singapore
i've never been to singapore
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have / I've never been to Singapore. 'I have never went' = 40 (past form). 'I haven't never been' = 60 (never is already negative). 'I have never gone to Singapore' = 60 (been to = went and came back). 'I never been' = 40 (missing have). 'I haven't been to Singapore' = 70 (right meaning, but without never).

assessment.prompt: Add 'already' in the right place: I have paid the electricity bill.
acceptableAnswers: i have already paid the electricity bill
i've already paid the electricity bill
i have paid the electricity bill already
i've paid the electricity bill already
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have already paid the electricity bill (already at the end is also fine). 'I already have paid' = 60 (already goes after have). 'Already I have paid' = 50. 'I have paid already the electricity bill' = 50. 'I already paid' = 60 (American past simple; the task keeps have).

assessment.prompt: Translate with 'yet': Budi belum makan siang.
acceptableAnswers: budi hasn't had lunch yet
budi has not had lunch yet
budi hasn't eaten lunch yet
budi has not eaten lunch yet
budi hasn't had his lunch yet
budi has not had his lunch yet
budi hasn't eaten his lunch yet
budi has not eaten his lunch yet
assessment.rubric: Correct: Budi hasn't had lunch yet ('eaten lunch' and 'his lunch' also fine). 'Budi hasn't eat lunch yet' = 50. 'Budi haven't had lunch yet' = 60 (Budi → hasn't). 'Budi has had lunch yet' = 20 (positive, and yet only goes in negatives and questions). 'Budi hasn't yet had lunch' = 70 (possible but formal; yet usually at the end). Missing 'yet' = 70.

assessment.prompt: Translate with 'just': Saya baru saja makan.
acceptableAnswers: i have just eaten
i've just eaten
i have just had a meal
i've just had a meal
i have just had something to eat
i've just had something to eat
assessment.rubric: Correct: I have / I've just eaten. 'I just have eaten' = 60 (just goes after have). 'I have just ate' = 40 (past form instead of the third form). 'I just ate' = 60 (American past simple; the task asks for have + third form). 'I just eat' = 20.

blocks.text:
Indonesian talks about experiences and news with **pernah**, **sudah**, **belum** and **baru saja**, and the verb never changes. English uses a new form for this, the **present perfect**: **have/has + the third form** of the verb. It's for something that happened **before now** when you **don't say the exact time**, and it matters now: *I have finished* (so I'm free now).

- **have** with I, you, we, they; **has** with he, she, it (*Rina has*, like *Rina has a car*).
- Every verb has **three forms**: the base (bentuk dasar, the dictionary form), the past (bentuk kedua) and the **third form** (bentuk ketiga, in English the **past participle**).
- **Regular verbs** (the -ed verbs): the third form looks **the same as the past**: *work → worked → worked*.
- Some **irregular verbs** have a **new** third form. They are exceptions with no rule: learn these seven by heart.

id.text:
Bahasa Indonesia membicarakan pengalaman dan kabar baru dengan **pernah**, **sudah**, **belum** dan **baru saja**, dan kata kerjanya tidak pernah berubah. Bahasa Inggris memakai bentuk baru untuk ini, yaitu **present perfect**: **have/has + bentuk ketiga** kata kerja. Bentuk ini untuk hal yang terjadi **sebelum sekarang** saat kamu **tidak menyebut waktunya**, dan hasilnya penting sekarang: *I have finished* (jadi sekarang saya sudah bebas).

- **have** untuk I, you, we, they; **has** untuk he, she, it (*Rina has*, seperti *Rina has a car*).
- Setiap kata kerja punya **tiga bentuk**: bentuk dasar (bentuk kamus), bentuk lampau (bentuk kedua) dan **bentuk ketiga** (dalam bahasa Inggris disebut **past participle**).
- **Kata kerja beraturan** (yang memakai -ed): bentuk ketiganya **sama dengan bentuk lampau**: *work → worked → worked*.
- Beberapa **kata kerja tidak beraturan** punya bentuk ketiga yang **baru**. Ini pengecualian tanpa aturan: hafalkan tujuh kata ini.

rows.note: new verb: written has double t

id.note: kata kerja baru: written memakai dua t

rows.note: same as the past: I've had lunch (the first have is the helper)

id.note: sama dengan bentuk lampau: I've had lunch (have yang pertama adalah kata bantu)

rows.note: same as the past (also: made, said)

id.note: sama dengan bentuk lampau (juga: made, said)

blocks.text: Two common mistakes. Using the **past** after have/has: 'I have saw that film' → **I have seen that film**. And forgetting **has**: 'She have finished' → **She has finished**. Short forms: **I've, you've, we've, they've**; **he's, she's, it's** = has when a third form follows (*She's eaten*), but = is before -ing (*She's eating*). Negative: **haven't / hasn't** (= have not / has not) + third form. Question: **Have you…? Has she…?** + third form.

id.text: Dua kesalahan yang sering terjadi. Memakai **bentuk lampau** setelah have/has: 'I have saw that film' → **I have seen that film**. Dan lupa memakai **has**: 'She have finished' → **She has finished**. Bentuk singkat: **I've, you've, we've, they've**; **he's, she's, it's** = has kalau diikuti bentuk ketiga (*She's eaten*), tapi = is kalau diikuti -ing (*She's eating*). Negatif: **haven't / hasn't** (= have not / has not) + bentuk ketiga. Pertanyaan: **Have you…? Has she…?** + bentuk ketiga.

blocks.prompt: We ___ a new rice cooker. The old one doesn't work.
blocks.explain: We → have, and buy → bought → bought (the third form is the same as the past). 'buyed' adds -ed to an irregular verb, and 'has' is for he, she, it.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: We ___ a new rice cooker. The old one doesn't work.
id.explain: We → have, dan buy → bought → bought (bentuk ketiganya sama dengan bentuk lampau). 'buyed' menambah -ed pada kata kerja tidak beraturan, dan 'has' untuk he, she, it.

blocks.text:
To ask about someone's **life experience**, use **Have you ever + third form?** (**ever** = pernah, at any time in your life). Short answers: **Yes, I have.** / **No, I haven't.** / **No, never.** To say 'belum pernah' or 'tidak pernah', use **never**: *I have never eaten durian.* **never** already means 'not', so don't add another not: 'I haven't never…' is wrong.

**The Indonesian trap:** *Saya pernah ke Bali* has *pernah*, but in English a positive sentence has **no ever**: **I have been to Bali** (not 'I have ever been'). **ever** is for questions.

**Why been, not went?** For places, English says **have been to** = went there and came back. **been** is the third form of *be* (be → was/were → been). **went** is the past form, and after have/has you always need the third form, so 'Have you ever went…?' is wrong.

id.text:
Untuk bertanya tentang **pengalaman hidup** seseorang, pakai **Have you ever + bentuk ketiga?** (**ever** = pernah, kapan saja dalam hidupmu). Jawaban singkat: **Yes, I have.** / **No, I haven't.** / **No, never.** Untuk bilang 'belum pernah' atau 'tidak pernah', pakai **never**: *I have never eaten durian.* **never** sudah berarti 'tidak', jadi jangan tambah not lagi: 'I haven't never…' itu salah.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** *Saya pernah ke Bali* memakai *pernah*, tapi di bahasa Inggris kalimat positif **tidak memakai ever**: **I have been to Bali** (bukan 'I have ever been'). **ever** untuk pertanyaan.

**Kenapa been, bukan went?** Untuk tempat, bahasa Inggris bilang **have been to** = pernah pergi ke sana dan sudah kembali. **been** adalah bentuk ketiga dari *be* (be → was/were → been). **went** itu bentuk lampau, dan setelah have/has selalu perlu bentuk ketiga, jadi 'Have you ever went…?' itu salah.

rows.en: Have you ever been to Lombok? — Yes, I have.
Has Rina ever seen a volcano? — No, she hasn't.
rows.id: Rina pernah melihat gunung berapi? — Belum.
Saya sudah dua kali ke Malaysia.

rows.en: My father has never been on a plane.

blocks.text: **been** or **gone**? Both are third forms, but the meaning is different. *Budi has **been** to Bali* = he went there and came back (pernah ke Bali). *Budi has **gone** to Bali* = he went and he is in Bali now (sedang di Bali, belum pulang). For experiences, you almost always need **been**.

id.text: **been** atau **gone**? Keduanya bentuk ketiga, tapi artinya berbeda. *Budi has **been** to Bali* = dia pernah ke sana dan sudah kembali (pernah ke Bali). *Budi has **gone** to Bali* = dia pergi dan sekarang ada di Bali (sedang di Bali, belum pulang). Untuk pengalaman, hampir selalu pakai **been**.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence means 'Saya pernah ke Surabaya'?
options: I have ever been to Surabaya.
blocks.explain: pernah ke = have been to. A positive sentence has no ever (ever is for questions), and after have you need the third form been, not the past went.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang artinya 'Saya pernah ke Surabaya'?
id.explain: pernah ke = have been to. Kalimat positif tidak memakai ever (ever untuk pertanyaan), dan setelah have perlu bentuk ketiga been, bukan bentuk lampau went.

blocks.text:
The present perfect **doesn't say when**. As soon as you say a **finished time**, English switches back to the **past simple** (went, saw, ate): **yesterday, last night, last week, last year, two days ago**, and questions with **When…?**

So 'I have seen it yesterday' is wrong: say **I saw it yesterday.** This is a trap for Indonesian speakers, because *sudah* goes with *kemarin* without a problem: *Kemarin saya sudah ke dokter* = **I went to the doctor yesterday** (past simple, because of yesterday).

A real conversation often **starts** with the present perfect (the experience) and gives the **details** in the past simple (when, where, with whom).

id.text:
Present perfect **tidak menyebut kapan**. Begitu kamu menyebut **waktu yang sudah selesai**, bahasa Inggris kembali ke **past simple** (went, saw, ate): **yesterday, last night, last week, last year, two days ago**, dan pertanyaan dengan **When…?**

Jadi 'I have seen it yesterday' itu salah: ucapkan **I saw it yesterday.** Ini jebakan untuk penutur bahasa Indonesia, karena *sudah* bisa dipakai bersama *kemarin*: *Kemarin saya sudah ke dokter* = **I went to the doctor yesterday** (past simple, karena ada yesterday).

Percakapan sehari-hari sering **dimulai** dengan present perfect (pengalamannya), lalu **detailnya** memakai past simple (kapan, di mana, dengan siapa).

rows.en: Have you ever eaten gudeg? — Yes, I have. I ate it in Yogyakarta last year.
rows.id: Kamu pernah makan gudeg? — Pernah. Saya makan gudeg di Yogyakarta tahun lalu.
rows.note: experience → present perfect; when → past simple

id.note: pengalaman → present perfect; kapan → past simple

rows.en: I've seen this film. I saw it two weeks ago.
rows.id: Saya sudah nonton film ini. Saya nonton dua minggu lalu.

rows.en: When did you go to Bali?

blocks.text: Quick test: is there a **finished time** in the sentence (yesterday, last…, … ago)? Yes → **past simple**. No time, and it's about your life or fresh news → **have/has + third form**.

id.text: Tes cepat: apakah ada **waktu yang sudah selesai** di kalimatnya (yesterday, last…, … ago)? Ada → **past simple**. Tidak ada waktu, dan isinya tentang pengalaman hidup atau kabar baru → **have/has + bentuk ketiga**.

blocks.explain: two days ago is a finished time, so use the past simple: called. 'have called' can't go with ago, and 'have call' is missing the third form.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: I ___ Rina two days ago.
id.explain: two days ago adalah waktu yang sudah selesai, jadi pakai past simple: called. 'have called' tidak bisa dipakai dengan ago, dan 'have call' tidak memakai bentuk ketiga.

id.title: Ada kata yesterday? Pakai past simple

blocks.text:
These three words are for **fresh news**, and they match Indonesian words you use every day:
- **just** = baru saja: *The bus has **just** left.*
- **already** = sudah (often sooner than expected): *I've **already** done my homework.*
- **not … yet** = belum: *I haven't paid **yet**.* In questions, **yet** = sudah … belum?: *Have you eaten **yet**?*

**Where do they go?** **just** and **already** go **between have/has and the third form**. **yet** goes **at the end**, and only in **negatives and questions**. Answers: **Yes, I have.** / **No, not yet.**

So *Sudah makan belum?* = **Have you eaten yet?** and the answer *Belum* = **No, not yet.**

id.text:
Tiga kata ini untuk **kabar baru**, dan cocok dengan kata bahasa Indonesia yang kamu pakai setiap hari:
- **just** = baru saja: *The bus has **just** left.*
- **already** = sudah (sering lebih cepat dari dugaan): *I've **already** done my homework.*
- **not … yet** = belum: *I haven't paid **yet**.* Di pertanyaan, **yet** = sudah … belum?: *Have you eaten **yet**?*

**Di mana letaknya?** **just** dan **already** diletakkan **di antara have/has dan bentuk ketiga**. **yet** diletakkan **di akhir**, dan hanya di **kalimat negatif dan pertanyaan**. Jawabannya: **Yes, I have.** / **No, not yet.**

Jadi *Sudah makan belum?* = **Have you eaten yet?** dan jawaban *Belum* = **No, not yet.**

rows.note: yet at the end of a negative

rows.en: Has the package arrived yet? — No, not yet.
rows.note: yet at the end of a question

blocks.text: Indonesian *Saya sudah selesai PR* has no helper word, so learners write 'I already finish my homework'. English needs **have + third form**: **I've already finished my homework.** Don't put yet in a positive sentence ('I have finished yet' is wrong). British vs American: Americans often use the past simple with these words (*I just ate. Did you eat yet?*). Both are understood; in this course we use the have/has form.

id.text: *Saya sudah selesai PR* tidak memakai kata bantu, jadi pelajar sering menulis 'I already finish my homework'. Bahasa Inggris perlu **have + bentuk ketiga**: **I've already finished my homework.** Jangan pakai yet di kalimat positif ('I have finished yet' itu salah). British vs Amerika: orang Amerika sering memakai past simple dengan kata-kata ini (*I just ate. Did you eat yet?*). Keduanya dimengerti; di kursus ini kita memakai bentuk have/has.

blocks.explain: hasn't = a negative, and 'belum' in a negative is yet, at the end. already and just go in positive sentences, between has and the third form.

id.explain: hasn't = kalimat negatif, dan 'belum' di kalimat negatif adalah yet, di akhir. already dan just dipakai di kalimat positif, di antara has dan bentuk ketiga.

id.intro: Hai! Kamu sudah bisa bercerita tentang kemarin dengan went, saw dan ate. Sekarang kamu belajar bentuk baru untuk pengalaman dan kabar terbaru: I've been to Bali. I've just finished. Have you eaten yet? Pemanasan: kamu pernah ke Bali? Coba jawab 'Yes, I have.' atau 'No, I haven't.'
suggestedQuestions: Kenapa 'Have you ever been to Bali?', bukan 'Have you ever went'?
Apa bedanya 'I saw it' dan 'I have seen it'?
Bagaimana bilang 'Sudah makan belum?' dalam bahasa Inggris?
Di mana letak just, already dan yet dalam kalimat?

assessment.ppf-1: Lengkapi dengan present perfect dari 'take': Rina ___ a lot of photos of the new office.
assessment.ppf-2: Perbaiki kesalahannya: I have seen Dimas at the mall yesterday.
assessment.ppf-3: Tulis pertanyaan dalam bahasa Inggris dengan 'ever' (Kamu pernah melihat komodo?): you / see / a Komodo dragon
assessment.ppf-4: Terjemahkan ke bahasa Inggris dengan 'never': Saya belum pernah ke Singapura.
assessment.ppf-5: Tambahkan 'already' di tempat yang benar: I have paid the electricity bill.
assessment.ppf-6: Terjemahkan ke bahasa Inggris dengan 'yet': Budi belum makan siang.
assessment.ppf-7: Terjemahkan ke bahasa Inggris dengan 'just': Saya baru saja makan.
